question: A 50-year-old man completed triple therapy for H. pylori eradication 4 weeks ago. Which test is most appropriate to confirm successful eradication?

answers.text: Urea breath test (UBT) performed after stopping PPI for at least 2 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The UBT detects active urease from live organisms and is the preferred non-invasive eradication test. It must be done ≥4 weeks after antibiotics and ≥2 weeks after stopping PPIs, as PPIs suppress bacterial urease activity causing false negatives.

answers.text: Serum IgG ELISA for H. pylori antibodies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IgG serology remains positive for months to years after successful eradication due to immunological memory. It cannot distinguish active from past infection and is useless for confirming cure.

answers.text: Rapid urease test (CLO test) on endoscopic antral biopsy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The CLO test requires invasive endoscopy — not indicated as first-line when a non-invasive test (UBT) is available. Reserve for patients needing repeat endoscopy for other clinical indications.
Pepsinogen ratios reflect gastric mucosal atrophy and are used for gastric cancer screening. They do not directly detect H. pylori or its metabolic activity and cannot confirm eradication.

overallFeedback.feedback: For eradication confirmation: UBT (or stool antigen test) — both detect active infection. Never use serology (stays positive after cure). Stop PPI ≥2 weeks before testing to avoid false negatives.
UBT is the gold-standard non-invasive eradication test. Timing matters: ≥4 weeks post-antibiotics, ≥2 weeks off PPI.
